question:
Patient note:
A 56-year-old man with well-controlled hypertension on lisinopril 20 mg daily and longstanding gastroesophageal reflux for which he takes over-the-counter famotidine presented to the emergency department at 05:50 after a frightening episode at home in which he abruptly lost consciousness while walking from the bathroom to the kitchen; his spouse, who witnessed the event, reported that he toppled forward without bracing, remained motionless for roughly fifteen seconds, then regained awareness confused but able to answer questions. He recalls feeling light-headed and hearing a “roaring” in his ears seconds before the blackout but denies chest tightness, palpitations, or seeing flashing lights. Ten minutes prior to the spell he had vomited a basinful of maroon-tinged fluid mixed with partly digested dinner remnants; a second smaller retch occurred in the car on the way to hospital, again described as streaked dark red material with no foul tarry odor and no clotted black stool in the sink or toilet. His last bowel movement yesterday afternoon was normal medium brown; none since. He denies bright red blood per rectum, shiny black stools, abdominal distension, pruritus, jaundice, ankle swelling, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, orthopnea, easy bruising, fevers, chills, or weight loss. He has never undergone upper endoscopy, takes no non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, corticosteroids, antiplatelet agents, or anticoagulants, drinks alcohol only at holiday gatherings, quit smoking fifteen years ago after a 20-pack-year history, and has no illicit drug use. Family history is notable for a father who died of myocardial infarction at 72 and a sister with celiac disease; there is no known bleeding diathesis. On arrival—before any intravenous line was started, before antiemetic, acid suppression, fluids, blood products, or vasoactive medications—he sat upright on the stretcher, alert and oriented, skin slightly pale and clammy but speaking in complete sentences. Manual triage vitals documented a blood pressure of 106/64 mm Hg in the right arm at heart level, a regular pulse of 80 beats per minute confirmed on three-lead monitor, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oral temperature 36.9 °C, and oxygen saturation 97 % on ambient air. Capillary refill was about three seconds; conjunctivae were mildly pale, sclerae anicteric, oral mucosa moist with a thin coffee-ground coating at the soft palate. Neck veins were not distended at 45°, carotid pulses were brisk without bruits, and peripheral pulses were 2+ symmetric without lower-extremity edema. Cardiac auscultation revealed a regular rhythm with crisp S1 and S2, no murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Lungs were clear to auscultation bilaterally. The abdomen was flat, nondistended, and demonstrated moderate tenderness in the epigastrium and left upper quadrant without guarding or rebound; no palpable masses, organomegaly, or ascites were appreciated, and bowel sounds were hyperactive. Skin inspection showed no spider angiomata, palmar erythema, petechiae, or ecchymoses. Focused neurologic examination revealed equal and reactive pupils, intact extraocular movements, 5/5 strength in all extremities, and normal finger-to-nose testing; there was no residual focal deficit from the earlier faint. A bedside guaiac performed on a small sample of emesis was positive for occult blood; digital rectal examination, deferred until after labs were drawn because the patient felt nauseated, was later negative for pigmented stool. Two 18-gauge peripheral catheters were placed exclusively for blood sampling; at that moment no therapeutic infusions, transfusions, proton-pump inhibitors, or antiemetics had been administered. Initial laboratory studies obtained ten minutes after presentation and prior to intervention revealed hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL, hematocrit 34 %, mean corpuscular volume 92 fL, platelet count 228 × 10⁹/L, white blood cell count 9.1 × 10⁹/L, blood urea nitrogen 55 mg/dL, serum creatinine 1.2 mg/dL (baseline 1.1), sodium 138 mEq/L, potassium 4.0 mEq/L, chloride 103 mEq/L, bicarbonate 24 mEq/L, glucose 112 mg/dL, international normalized ratio 1.05, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, AST 29 U/L, ALT 31 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 96 U/L, and albumin 4.1 g/dL. A 12-lead electrocardiogram recorded concurrently demonstrated normal sinus rhythm at 78 bpm with normal intervals and no ischemic changes. Upright chest radiography showed clear lung fields and a normal cardiac silhouette, and an abdominal series revealed a nonspecific gas pattern without free air. The patient remained nil per os, was placed on continuous cardiac and pulse-oximetry monitoring, and type and screen for packed red blood cells was sent while gastroenterology consultation was requested for expedited esophagogastroduodenoscopy to localize and control the suspected upper gastrointestinal source of bleeding identified prior to any resuscitative treatment.

Question: What is the patient's Glasgow-Blatchford Bleeding score? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Glasgow-Blatchford Bleeding Score uses admission BUN, sex-specific hemoglobin, systolic pressure, pulse, melena, syncope, hepatic disease and cardiac failure.
- BUN 55 mg/dL (urea ≈19.6 mmol/L): in the 10 to <25 mmol/L urea band = 4.
- Hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL in a man: 10 to <12 g/dL = 3.
- Systolic pressure 106 mmHg: 100–109 mmHg = 1.
- Pulse 80/min: below 100/min = 0.
- Melena absent: stool was brown; bloody emesis is not melena = 0.
- Syncope: witnessed transient loss of consciousness = 2.
- Hepatic disease: none reported = 0.
- Cardiac failure: none reported = 0.
Sum: 4 + 3 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 2 + 0 + 0 = 10.
Final answer: 10
